answers.transcript:
Okay, so I want to talk about my cousin Emre, he is a mathematics teacher.
He is only five years older than me but he explain everything very good.
In the last year of the lycee I had a big problem with the mathematic.
My teacher explained one time and after that he pass to the next subject.
But my cousin, he sit with me in the kitchen table and he draw the problem in a paper.
He always start with a easy example from the daily life, for example the football.
After that he make the question more difficult, step by step, until I understand.
He never say to me that this question is easy, and this is very important.
I passed my exam in the end and now I use the same method with my little sister.
I find his way helpful because he is patient and he never makes me feel stupid.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: All three points on the card and the closing question enter in sequence, and the talk does not break off; but each point ends in a single sentence and transitions never go beyond the pattern "After that", "for example", "because". The section on how the cousin explained is skimmed in three sentences, and a single lesson scene is never opened up.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Vocabulary describing the act of explaining stays in the everyday core: explain, example, easy, difficult, patient repeat, and emphasis is made with "very good", "very important". "Step by step" stands alone; there is no second collocation of the kind the card would call for.
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Agreement errors are in most sentences and repeat in the same form (he explain, he pass, he sit, he draw, he start, he make, he never say), alongside article errors (a easy, the mathematic) and preposition errors (in the kitchen table, in a paper); meaning is still never closed off. Structures are simple, with no complex structure beyond the when and because clauses.

answers.what_would_lift_it: Show from start to finish how the cousin explained a single topic — which question, what was said first, what was drawn next — because at present the method is summarised under the headings "easy example" and "step by step". In the language, first fix the third-person -s, since the same error repeats in every sentence of the response.

answers.transcript:
So the person I'm going to talk about is my cousin Emre, who is a maths teacher.
He's only five years older than me, so when I was in my last year at high school he was already teaching.
At that time I was having serious problems with maths, especially with derivatives.
The problem was, my teacher at school explained the topic only once and then he passed directly to the next chapter.
My cousin was completely different, he used to sit with me at the kitchen table for two or three hours in the weekend.
The first thing he always did was to break the problem down into small pieces, and he never started from the formula.
For example, he explained the derivative with the speed of a car, and suddenly the whole subject was making sense for me.
Another thing, he never said me that a question is easy, because when somebody says this you feel even more stupid.
In the end I got a good result in the exam, and now I use the same method with my sister.
So the reason I find his way helpful is simple, he thinks about the person in front of him, not about himself.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: All three points are developed and the comparison between the school teacher and the cousin carries the narrative; the derivative example is concrete and well placed. The flow becomes mechanical: sections open in the same pattern with "The problem was", "The first thing", "Another thing", "So the reason", and sentences run at the same length.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: There is vocabulary to carry the topic (break the problem down into small pieces, make sense, derivatives, a good result), and meaning is never closed off. Phrasing flattens in two places: "making sense for me", "I got a good result in the exam".
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: A relative clause, "used to", the past continuous and the emphatic structure built with "the first thing he did was" are controlled; more than two-thirds of sentences are error-free. The remaining errors sit in a narrow set: preposition (in the weekend, make sense for), verb pattern (he never said me).

answers.what_would_lift_it: Run the derivative example one sentence further: the idea of the car's speed is the response's best part but is left in a single sentence. In the language, fixing the "say something to somebody" pattern and the preposition "at the weekend" is enough; the rest of the structure is already solid.

answers.transcript:
So, someone who's good at explaining things. That would be my cousin Emre, who teaches maths at a state school about an hour outside the city.
He's only five years older than me, which meant that when I was in my final year and completely at sea with maths, he'd already been teaching for two years.
And I was struggling, genuinely. My teacher at school would go through a topic once, at a hundred miles an hour, and then move straight on whether anyone had followed it or not.
Emre took a completely different approach. He'd come round at the weekend, sit down at the kitchen table with me, and, well, not even open the textbook at first.
What he does is break the thing down into pieces small enough that you can't get them wrong, and he never starts with the formula.
Derivatives, for instance. He explained the whole thing through a car speeding up and slowing down, and it just clicked. Ten minutes, after months of getting nowhere.
The other thing, and this is the real skill, is that he never once told me a question was easy. Because the moment somebody says that, you feel like an idiot for not seeing it.
I scraped through that exam in the end, and these days I catch myself using his tricks on my little sister.
Why it works, I suppose, is that he explains it for whoever is sitting in front of him, not for himself.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The narrative builds its own order: the school teacher is set up as a contrast, then the method is shown through a single example (derivatives), and the closing gathers the method into one sentence. There is one self-correction ("and, well, not even open the textbook at first"), the rare kind of pause that eight lines allow.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Less common items are plentiful and in place: completely at sea with, at a hundred miles an hour, move straight on, come round, break the thing down, it just clicked, months of getting nowhere, scraped through, catch myself using his tricks. The register is spoken throughout.
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Structural range is wide: the past perfect continuous (he'd already been teaching), habitual "would" (would go through a topic once), an indirect question with "whether anyone had followed it or not", a result structure with "pieces small enough that you can't get them wrong". There is no countable error.

answers.what_would_lift_it: This is on target; for the next level up, the closing judgement "he explains it for whoever is sitting in front of him" needs to be backed with a second person — what changes when the same method is applied to his sibling. There is nothing left to do in the language.
